pedagogy.summary: This topic pairs a naming task (the four human tooth types — incisors, canines, premolars, molars) with a powerful organising idea: SHAPE IS LINKED TO FUNCTION. Sharp flat-edged incisors at the front cut/bite, pointed canines tear, and broad bumpy premolars and molars at the back grind. The best teaching lets children feel this in their own mouth (run a tongue along the front vs back teeth) and then extends the shape–function rule across animals: herbivores have flat grinding teeth for plants, carnivores have sharp teeth for meat, and humans — omnivores — have ALL types because we eat both. The comparison is what makes the idea stick and connects to diet and to the mouth-stage of digestion. Keep function tied to a demonstrable action (cut, tear, grind) rather than an abstract label, and treat the animal comparison as evidence for the rule, not a separate fact to memorise.
bestPractices: Use the child's own mouth as the manipulative: feel and look at the sharp front incisors, the pointier canines, and the wide bumpy back molars, then link each shape to what it does when eating an apple.
Teach shape→function as a rule, then TEST it on animals: predict a rabbit's vs a lion's teeth from their diet, then check — turning the comparison into reasoning, not recall.
Demonstrate the function with a real bite: incisors cut into an apple, molars grind it — so 'cut/tear/grind' are actions the child performs, not words.
Frame humans as omnivores to explain WHY we have all four types — the punchline that ties diet, teeth and the animal comparison together.
Distinguish tooth TYPES (this topic) from tooth CARE/decay (a diet/health topic) so the shape–function idea stays in focus.
keyRepresentations: Labelled mouth/jaw map with the four types grouped by position (front cutters → back grinders)
The child's own teeth felt with tongue/mirror as primary evidence
Shape→action pairing: incisor=cut, canine=tear, premolar/molar=grind, each with the bite it performs

commonMisconceptions: 'All teeth are the same / just different sizes' — missing that different shapes do different jobs.
'Canines/'fangs' are for biting food hardest' — conflating pointiness with power; canines TEAR, the flat molars do the heavy grinding.
'Front teeth grind and back teeth cut' — reversing the position–function mapping.
'Carnivores have flat teeth because they're big animals' — linking tooth shape to size rather than to diet.
'Humans have special teeth unlike animals' — missing that we share the same tooth types and that having all of them marks us as omnivores.
'Teeth grow back if lost' at this age — confusing the one milk-to-adult replacement with unlimited regrowth (a common aside worth correcting).

learn.summary: Children learn the four human tooth types (incisors, canines, premolars, molars) and the organising idea that TOOTH SHAPE IS LINKED TO FUNCTION: flat-edged incisors cut/bite, pointed canines tear, and broad bumpy premolars and molars grind. The anchor is the child's own mouth as evidence — feeling sharp front teeth versus wide bumpy back teeth — paired with linking each shape to a demonstrable action on food. The idea is extended and tested across animals (herbivore flat grinders, carnivore sharp tearers) and lands on humans as omnivores who have ALL types because we eat both plants and meat. The animal comparison is treated as reasoning/evidence for the rule, not a separate fact to memorise.

activities.title: Feel and map your own teeth
feedback: If a learner says all teeth are the same shape, ask them to press a fingertip or tongue on a front tooth edge then a back tooth surface and describe each: one is a thin edge, the other is wide and bumpy.
If position and function are reversed (front grinds, back cuts), bite into an apple: the thin front edges slice in; the wide back teeth are what you chew with.
Reinforce 'cut / tear / grind' as actions the child performs, not just words to recall.
activities.rationale: Year 4 pupils are expected to identify the different types of teeth in humans and their simple functions; tying each type to a demonstrable action on food keeps function concrete rather than an abstract label.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils should identify the different types of teeth in humans and their simple functions.

Humans have four tooth types — incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding) — and tooth shape relates to diet, with herbivores, carnivores and omnivores having characteristically different dentition.
learnerActions: Run your tongue along the front teeth, then the back teeth, and notice the difference: sharp flat front edges versus wide bumpy back surfaces; look with a mirror if available.
On a mouth/jaw map, locate and name the four types grouped by position: incisors and canines at the front, premolars and molars toward the back.
For each type, say what it does when eating: incisor = cut/slice, canine = grip and tear, premolar/molar = crush and grind.
activities.intendedInsight: Teeth are not all the same — different shapes at different positions do different jobs, and you can feel this evidence in your own mouth.

activities.title: Apple-eating sequence: which tooth does which job
feedback: A common error is thinking the pointed canines ('fangs') do the hardest food work. Clarify: points are good for gripping and tearing, but flat wide molars do the heavy grinding.
If a learner matches grinding to a pointed tooth, ask: could you crush a nut more easily on a sharp point or on a wide flat surface?
activities.rationale: Linking shape to a performed action (rather than a memorised label) targets the misconception that pointiness means power and keeps function demonstrable.
sourceClaims: Humans have four tooth types — incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding) — and tooth shape relates to diet, with herbivores, carnivores and omnivores having characteristically different dentition.
learnerActions: Watch or describe eating a bite of apple and identify which teeth do each step: incisors slice in, then premolars and molars crush and grind.
Match each tooth type to the food-action it performs (cut, tear, grind).
Explain why the flat back molars — not the pointed canines — do the heavy grinding.
activities.intendedInsight: The job a tooth does follows from its shape: thin edges cut, points tear, flat bumpy surfaces grind.

activities.title: Predict an animal's teeth from its diet
feedback: If a learner reverses the mapping (flat teeth for the meat-eater, sharp for the grass-eater), contrast the actions: tearing meat needs points; grinding tough grass needs flat surfaces — then re-match.
If a learner links tooth shape to body size ('big animals have flat teeth'), redirect to diet: compare two differently sized herbivores, or a large carnivore, to show size is not the driver.
If a learner says the two mouths would look the same, revisit the shape→action rule before predicting again.
activities.rationale: Turning the comparison into predict-then-check makes it reasoning rather than recall and directly surfaces the reverse-mapping and size-not-diet misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Humans have four tooth types — incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding) — and tooth shape relates to diet, with herbivores, carnivores and omnivores having characteristically different dentition.
learnerActions: Before seeing the answer, predict what a grass-eating animal's teeth look like and what a meat-eating animal's teeth look like, and say why.

Check predictions against examples: a herbivore (e.g. a sheep or cow) with mostly flat wide cheek teeth for grinding tough plants; a carnivore (e.g. a lion) with sharp pointed tearers. (Notes: a rabbit is a herbivore too, but also has large front incisors for gnawing, so sheep and cow show the flat-grinder pattern most clearly; the fox is often used as a simple meat-eater but is actually a dietary omnivore, so the lion is the cleaner carnivore example.)

Answer a probe such as: a cow has no teeth at all at the front top of its mouth (just a hard pad) and no sharp pointed tearing teeth — what does that tell you it probably does NOT eat? And why would sharp tearing teeth be no good for an animal eating grass all day?
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape matches the job the diet needs, so you can reason from a diet to likely teeth (and from teeth back to likely diet).

activities.title: Read your own diet off your own teeth: why humans are omnivores
feedback: Full reasoning: links shape to function across animals AND explains humans have all types because omnivores eat both, reasoning from a new animal's teeth to its likely diet.

Partial: names tooth types and jobs, or compares herbivore and carnivore teeth, but treats them separately without connecting human mixed dentition to being an omnivore — prompt: 'If one shape means one food, what do BOTH shapes mean?'
If a learner labels humans as carnivore or herbivore, read the evidence: both tooth shapes present means both foods eaten.
If the aside comes up that teeth 'grow back' if lost, clarify: humans have one milk-to-adult replacement, not unlimited regrowth.
Aside: if a learner suggests a fox as a meat-eater, note that foxes actually eat some plants (such as fruit) too, which is why the lion is used as the clearer meat-eater contrast.
activities.rationale: Reading mixed human dentition as evidence of an omnivore diet is the discriminating step that distinguishes genuine shape-to-function reasoning from separate recalled facts.
sourceClaims: Humans have four tooth types — incisors (cutting), canines (tearing), premolars and molars (grinding) — and tooth shape relates to diet, with herbivores, carnivores and omnivores having characteristically different dentition.
learnerActions: Note that your mouth has BOTH sharp pointed front teeth AND flat wide back teeth.
Reason backwards: having both tooth shapes is evidence that both kinds of food can be eaten — eating both plants and meat is what 'omnivore' means.
Explain why humans have all four tooth types, connecting it to eating both plants and meat.

Answer the two-tier prompt: 'A sheep eats plants such as grass and a lion eats meat — would their teeth look the same or different, and why? And what does it tell you that humans have both sharp front teeth and flat back teeth?'
activities.intendedInsight: Humans share the same tooth types as many other mammals; having all of them is evidence we are omnivores who eat both plants and meat — the punchline that ties diet, teeth and the animal comparison together.

constraints: Keep each function tied to a demonstrable action (cut, tear, grind) rather than an abstract label.
Treat the animal comparison as evidence for the shape→function rule, not a separate set of facts to memorise.
Distinguish tooth TYPES (this topic) from tooth CARE/decay, which is a diet/health topic, so the shape–function idea stays in focus.

Matching and quiz tasks (tooth→job, categorising animals by diet) are useful consolidation and assessment; recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning of reading human mixed dentition as evidence of an omnivore diet, so include at least one task where the child predicts or explains.

A tap-to-explore mouth map or sorting game is one way to make the shape→function link concrete; a static labelled jaw map, the child's own mouth, or real food can serve the same purpose. Interactive reveals (lift-the-flap animal comparison, drag-to-match, bite-the-apple reveal) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not required.

When using the rabbit as a herbivore example, acknowledge its prominent gnawing incisors; sheep or cow are cleaner illustrations of the flat-grinder pattern. Likewise, prefer the lion as the clean carnivore example, since the fox is dietarily an omnivore.
Avoid implying teeth regrow repeatedly; there is a single milk-to-adult replacement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D jaw as 'poor'/'adds nothing' and a quiz as assessment-leaning; these catalog fit rankings have been removed and recast as neutral medium choices with stated affordances, not universal pedagogical laws.

The Britannica source claim about human tooth types and diet-linked dentition is marked verified:false in the row; treated as established general content, but comparative efficacy of any particular medium is not asserted.

Animal examples vary between the pedagogy (rabbit/lion) and assessment (sheep/fox); both are retained as interchangeable illustrations, with the rabbit caveated because its large gnawing incisors can mislead the 'herbivore = flat grinders' point, and the fox caveated because it is dietarily an omnivore rather than a strict carnivore.
The milk-to-adult tooth replacement aside is included as a conservative correction to the 'teeth grow back' misconception noted in the source, without claiming new verification.
An in-role conversation/dentist framing from the original is noted only as an optional, unproven engagement option; its distinct pedagogical value is not established.

probeDeeper: Which of your own teeth do you use to bite into an apple, and which to chew it up? Feel them with your tongue.
A cow has almost no sharp pointed teeth at the front top of its mouth. What does that tell you about what it does NOT eat?
Why would sharp tearing teeth be no good for an animal that eats grass all day?
assess.correctAnswer: Different: the sheep (a herbivore) has mostly flat, wide teeth for grinding tough grass; the fox (a carnivore) has sharp, pointed teeth for tearing meat — tooth SHAPE matches the JOB the diet needs. Humans have both kinds because we are omnivores who eat plants and meat, so we need incisors and canines to cut and tear AND premolars and molars to grind.

errorPatterns.pattern: All teeth do the same job / tooth shape isn't linked to what an animal eats.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match shape to task with real examples — flat for grinding, sharp for tearing; have the child predict an animal's teeth from its food.
errorPatterns.distractor: Their teeth would look the same — teeth are just for eating, shape doesn't matter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the two mouths would look the same, or that shape doesn't matter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses shape and function — thinks meat-eaters have flat crushing teeth and plant-eaters have sharp ones.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the actions: tearing meat needs points; grinding grass needs flat surfaces. Re-match to each animal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The fox has flat teeth for crushing and the sheep has sharp teeth for grass.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns flat teeth to the fox and sharp teeth to the sheep.

errorPatterns.pattern: Labels humans as carnivores or herbivores rather than omnivores, missing what mixed teeth imply.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the evidence backwards: both tooth shapes present means both foods eaten — that is what omnivore means.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls humans one single type despite having both tooth shapes.

responseLevels.gap: Says teeth are all the same or that shape is unrelated to diet, or reverses which shape suits which food.
responseLevels.full: Links tooth shape to function across animals AND explains humans have all types because omnivores eat both — reasoning from a new animal's teeth to its likely diet.
responseLevels.partial: Names tooth types and jobs, OR compares herbivore and carnivore teeth, but treats them separately — doesn't connect human mixed dentition to being an omnivore.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A sheep eats only grass and a fox eats meat. If you looked inside their mouths, would their teeth look the same or different? Explain why. And what does it tell you that humans have BOTH sharp pointed teeth at the front AND flat wide teeth at the back?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks all teeth do the same job, or that shape is unrelated to diet, says the mouths would look the same. A child who reverses the shape–function link assigns flat teeth to the fox. Only the shape-to-function reasoner both predicts the difference AND reads human mixed dentition as evidence of an omnivore diet — which the tier-two question forces.
